client: I got a rejection letter from my dream university last week, and I honestly haven't been able to shake this feeling that I'm just not good enough. It's like everything I worked for over the past few years meant nothing, and now I don't even know what my future looks like. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help, and I want you to know that what you're feeling — that sense of "what was it all for?" — makes complete sense after working so hard toward something that mattered deeply to you. A rejection like this can feel like a verdict on your worth as a person, but I'd gently invite us to explore whether that's truly what it means, or whether that's a painful story your mind is telling you in a really difficult moment. What does "not being good enough" look like to you — is it about this one outcome, or does it connect to something you've felt before?

client: Honestly, it's not just this one thing. I've had this feeling before, like when I didn't make the varsity team in high school or when I got a lower grade than I expected on a big exam. It's like this rejection just confirmed something I've been quietly afraid of for a long time — that no matter how hard I try, I'm always going to fall short somehow.
therapist: It sounds like this rejection didn't just sting on its own — it landed on top of a fear that's been quietly building for years, which makes it feel so much heavier and more "true" than it might otherwise. In CBT, we call this kind of pattern a **core belief** — a deeply held idea about ourselves that starts collecting "evidence" over time, while we unconsciously ignore the moments that contradict it. I'm curious: when you think about those same years of hard work you mentioned, are there any moments where you *didn't* fall short — times you succeeded or grew — that this belief might be causing you to overlook?

client: I mean, yeah, I can think of some things — I did well in my AP classes, I got a leadership position in one of my clubs, and a few of my teachers wrote really strong recommendations for me. But when I try to hold onto those things right now, they just feel small compared to this rejection, like they don't really count the same way. I guess I'm not sure how just listing good things is supposed to change the way I actually feel inside.
therapist: You're raising something really important — this isn't about just making a list of good things and expecting the feeling to disappear, and I don't want you to think that's what we're doing here. What's worth noticing is that your mind is applying two very different standards: the rejection *counts completely*, while the AP classes, the leadership role, the teachers who believed in you enough to advocate for you *don't really count* — and that uneven weighing of evidence is actually the belief protecting itself, not reality. What do you think it would mean if those achievements *did* count just as much — what would that say about the "I always fall short" story?

client: I guess if those things counted equally, then the story wouldn't really hold up — like, I couldn't honestly say I "always" fall short if I also have real evidence of succeeding. But it's hard to actually believe that in my gut, you know? It feels like I'm just trying to talk myself into feeling better rather than facing something that might actually be true about me.
therapist: You've actually just done something really significant — you logically dismantled the "always fall short" belief yourself, and that matters even if it doesn't *feel* true yet, because in CBT we understand that insight often comes before the emotional shift, not at the same time. The worry that you're just "talking yourself into feeling better" is worth examining too — it assumes that the painful version of the story is automatically more honest or real, but why would the harsher interpretation of yourself be more trustworthy than the gentler, evidence-based one? What do you think makes it feel safer or more "honest" to believe the critical story about yourself than to take the more balanced one seriously?

client: That's a question I haven't really thought about before, and it's kind of uncomfortable to sit with. I think maybe if I believe the critical version, I can't be caught off guard or disappointed again — like if I already expect the worst from myself, rejections hurt less somehow. But saying it out loud like that, it sounds kind of exhausting, like I've been bracing for impact for years without even realizing it.
therapist: What you just uncovered is genuinely profound — that the critical voice wasn't really telling you the truth about yourself, it was actually trying to *protect* you, and it makes so much sense that your mind developed that strategy. But you named it beautifully: it's exhausting to live braced for impact, and the protection comes at a real cost — it means you can never fully let your own wins land or feel safe in your own efforts. I'm wondering, now that you can see that pattern more clearly, what might it feel like to experiment — even just a little — with letting your guard down and allowing the evidence of your strengths to actually count?

client: Honestly, the idea of letting my guard down feels kind of scary — like if I start believing in myself more and then get rejected again, it would hurt so much worse than it does now. I think part of me is wondering how you actually practice something like that in real life, because it sounds good in theory but I don't know what it would look like day to day. It's not like I can just decide to feel differently about myself overnight.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense — you're essentially being asked to take an emotional risk, and your mind has spent years building that protective wall for a reason. You're absolutely right that it doesn't happen overnight, but in practice it can start very small — things like pausing when you dismiss a success and asking "would I discount this if a close friend achieved it?", or gently noticing when the critical voice shows up without automatically believing everything it says. It's less about *deciding* to feel differently and more about slowly building tiny moments of evidence that it's safe to let good things count — so I'm curious, is there one small situation coming up where you might practice letting a strength or accomplishment actually land, even just for a moment?

client: There's actually a presentation I have to give next week for one of my classes, and I know I've prepared well for it — but I'm already anticipating that I'll find some way to pick it apart afterward even if it goes fine. I could try that thing you mentioned, asking myself if I'd dismiss it if a friend did the same work, but I'm a little worried I'll just go through the motions without it actually meaning anything. I guess my question is, what do I do if I try it and the critical voice just comes back louder?
therapist: It's really encouraging that you already have a concrete moment to practice with, and the fact that you're anticipating the self-criticism actually gives you a small advantage — you can almost set a gentle "watch" for it rather than being blindsided. When the critical voice does come back louder, the goal isn't to silence it or win an argument with it, but to notice it like a familiar pattern and ask "is this the protective voice doing its job again, or is this actually the truth?" — that small pause is the practice, even if it doesn't feel dramatic or transformative in the moment. After the presentation, I'd love to hear what you notice — not whether you "succeeded" at quieting the voice, but simply what it was like to observe it with a little more distance than usual.

client: I think I can try that — just observing it rather than fighting it feels a little less overwhelming than what I thought you were going to suggest. But I want to be honest, part of me is still worried that I'll get so caught up in how the presentation is going that I'll forget to even notice the voice until I'm already deep in the self-criticism spiral. Is it okay if the practice doesn't go perfectly, or does that just become another thing I end up feeling like I failed at?
therapist: It's such a meaningful question to ask, and I want to be really clear: if you only notice the critical voice *after* you're already in the spiral, that still counts as the practice — in fact, that's often exactly how it starts, and noticing it even five minutes later than you'd like is genuinely progress, not failure. There's something a little ironic and worth holding onto here: if you turned this practice itself into a pass/fail test, that would just be the same critical pattern showing up in a new outfit. What would it look like to treat this experiment with the same compassion you'd offer a friend who was trying something new and imperfect for the first time?

client: If a friend came to me and said they were trying this for the first time and didn't do it perfectly, I'd probably tell them that just making the effort matters and that it's okay to be a work in progress. But when I try to turn that same thought toward myself, there's this immediate resistance, like some part of me doesn't think I deserve that same kind of understanding. I guess that's kind of the whole point of what we've been talking about, isn't it — that I hold myself to a completely different standard than I'd hold anyone else.
therapist: You've just made one of the most important connections in this whole process — recognizing that the compassion you freely give to others is something you've been quietly withholding from yourself, and naming that so clearly takes real self-awareness. That gap between how you treat others and how you treat yourself isn't a character flaw; it's actually something that can be gradually closed with exactly the kind of practice we've been talking about, one small moment at a time. I'm wondering — what do you think it would mean for you, not just in this presentation but more broadly, if you slowly started treating yourself as someone who *deserves* the same understanding you'd give a friend?

client: Honestly, if I could actually do that, I think things might feel a lot less exhausting — like I wouldn't be fighting myself every time something doesn't go perfectly. But I'm sitting here realizing I don't even fully know what it feels like to believe I deserve that kind of understanding, because it's been so long since I've extended it to myself, if I ever really have. It's a little overwhelming to think about, like I'm being asked to rebuild something I'm not sure I ever had in the first place.
therapist: What you're sitting with right now is both heavy and quietly hopeful — because recognizing that this has been missing for a long time isn't the same as saying it can never be built, and in some ways, people who are building self-compassion for the first time have something powerful: they're choosing it consciously rather than just inheriting it. You don't have to rebuild it all at once or even know what it fully feels like yet — it can start as small as the moment after your presentation next week, when you try offering yourself the same words you'd give a friend. I want to ask: in your life right now, is there even one small area — however modest — where you already treat yourself with a little bit of that kindness, somewhere we might look to as a seed of what's already there?
